The chef

The question was simple.

Can a cake rise — truly rise — without eggs? Trained in professional hospitality and kitchens, I spent years testing, failing and refining until eggless stopped meaning less than. The result is a complete pâtisserie system: 129 recipes, 688 pages, and a book built like a professional reference. Chef. Author. Researcher — in that order, every single day.

The book

The Art of Eggless Pâtisserie — 688 pages, 129 recipes, zero eggs.

Every classic French dessert you were told needs eggs — the opera, the éclair, the mille-feuille, the silk-smooth mousse — rebuilt from the molecule up. This is not a book of substitutes. It is the complete science of eggless baking: what every ingredient actually does, why every step exists, and the exact technique that makes each recipe foolproof. Read it once, and you will never just follow a recipe again — you will understand it.

  • 129 restaurant-grade recipes, every one tested to professional standard
  • The science behind every step — so you can fix any recipe, not just follow one
  • Classic French pâtisserie — tarts, entremets, mousses, petits gâteaux — all eggless, all gelatin-free

The Oven Doesn't Lie

Recipes tell you what to do. This book tells you why — the hidden laws of heat, time, sugar and structure that separate a good baker from a great one. Every baker reaches a moment when recipes stop being enough, when you need to understand your oven instead of obeying it. This book is that moment, bound in pages. If the first book gave you the science, this one gives you the wisdom — and you will never bake on guesswork again. In writing now.

Eggless Gelatin-Free Gourmet Chocolate Mousse

Dark chocolate, set without eggs or gelatin — plated with chocolate crumble and berry gel.

Read the recipeDownload PDF
Eggless · Gelatin-free

Gourmet Chocolate Mousse

French-inspired · silky · airy · intensely chocolatey

Yield6 generous portions
StyleRestaurant / fine-dining pastry
StructureChocolate + whipped cream

Ingredients

Dark couverture200 g, 66–70%, finely chopped
Full-fat milk100 g
Glucose syrup20 g
Vanilla bean paste2 g
Espresso powder1 g
Fine sea salt1 g
Heavy / whipping cream300 g, 35%+ fat, very cold

Method

  1. Prepare the chocolate. Place finely chopped couverture in a dry heatproof bowl. The smaller and more uniform the pieces, the more evenly the ganache will emulsify.

  2. Heat the dairy. Combine milk, glucose, vanilla, espresso powder and salt in a saucepan. Heat gently to about 75–80°C. Do not boil aggressively.

  3. Build the ganache. Pour about one-third of the hot dairy over the chocolate. Rest 30 seconds. Stir from the centre outward with a spatula until a glossy elastic emulsion forms. Add the remaining hot dairy in two additions, fully emulsifying after each addition.

  4. Finish the emulsion. Blend with an immersion blender for about 30–45 seconds with the blade fully submerged. Keep the blade below the surface to avoid introducing air. The ganache should be perfectly smooth and glossy.

  5. Add cold cream. Add the 300 g very cold cream and blend briefly until completely homogeneous. The mixture should be fluid, glossy and uniform.

  6. Mature the mousse base. Cover the surface directly with cling film and refrigerate for at least 6 hours, preferably overnight. This allows the chocolate fat to crystallise and the base to become properly chilled before whipping.

  7. Whip. Transfer the fully chilled mixture to a chilled bowl. Whip at medium speed until soft-to-medium peaks form. Stop before the mousse becomes stiff, grainy or buttery.

  8. Check the texture. Lift the whisk. The mousse should hold a soft peak whose tip gently bends. It should be silky, airy and glossy — not dense like frosting and not liquid like ganache.

  9. Portion or plate. Pipe into serving glasses or form quenelles with two warm dessert spoons. For the cleanest quenelle, work with cold mousse and warm, dry spoons.

  10. Chill before serving. After portioning, refrigerate for 1–2 hours for a clean restaurant-style set. Serve chilled but not ice-cold so the chocolate aroma and melt are apparent.

Fine-dining plating suggestion

Chocolate mousse quenelle + raspberry gel + thin dark chocolate tuile + cocoa crumble + a few fresh raspberries + tiny flakes of sea salt. Keep the plate restrained: one dominant mousse element, one acidic fruit element, one crisp element and a small amount of texture. The goal is contrast — silky mousse, bright raspberry acidity, crisp chocolate and subtle cocoa bitterness.

Professional pastry notes

  • Chocolate: 66–70% couverture gives a balanced structure and intense flavour. Higher cocoa percentages will produce a firmer, more bitter mousse.
  • Cream: Use cream with at least 35% fat. Keep it very cold before the final emulsion and whipping.
  • Temperature: The base must be thoroughly chilled before whipping. If it is warm, it will not aerate properly.
  • Whipping: Medium speed gives better control than maximum speed. Stop as soon as the desired soft-to-medium peak is achieved.
  • No gelatin / no agar: The mousse is structured entirely by chocolate crystallisation and aerated cream.
  • Storage: Keep covered and refrigerated. For best texture and presentation, consume within 48 hours.
  • Texture target: silky and light on the tongue, stable enough to hold a quenelle, with no graininess or waxiness.

Curly Chef standard: eggless · gelatin-free · restaurant-style pastry technique

Eggless Sticky Toffee Pudding

Dark, date-rich sponge drowned in warm toffee sauce — the dates do the binding, so this one cannot fail.

Read the recipe
New recipe · Foolproof

Eggless Sticky Toffee Pudding

Dark, damp and unapologetically saucy — Britain’s greatest pudding, no eggs needed.

Makes8 generous portions
Bake175°C / 155°C fan, 30–35 min
Tin20 cm square, lined

Ingredients

Medjool dates, pitted200 g
Boiling water250 g
Baking soda5 g (1 tsp)
Unsalted butter, soft75 g, plus extra for the tin
Dark muscovado sugar150 g
Plain full-fat yogurt120 g
Vanilla bean paste5 g (1 tsp)
Plain flour190 g
Baking powder8 g (2 tsp)
Fine sea salt3 g

Toffee sauce

Unsalted butter100 g
Dark muscovado sugar150 g
Double cream200 g
Fine sea salt2 g
Vanilla bean paste5 g

Method

  1. Heat the oven to 175°C / 155°C fan. Butter and line the tin.

  2. Soak the dates. Put the dates in a heatproof bowl, pour over the boiling water and sprinkle over the baking soda. Rest 20 minutes until soft and dark, then blitz to a rough purée — a few lumps are fine.

  3. Cream the base. Beat the butter and muscovado sugar for 2–3 minutes until fluffy. Beat in the yogurt and vanilla.

  4. Add the dates. Stir the warm date purée into the creamed mixture until even.

  5. Fold the dries. Sift the flour, baking powder and salt over the bowl and fold gently until just combined.

  6. Bake. Scrape into the tin and level. Bake 30–35 minutes until risen, springy, and a skewer shows moist crumbs (not wet batter).

  7. Make the sauce. Melt the butter, muscovado sugar, cream and salt in a saucepan. Simmer 3 minutes, stirring, until slightly thickened and glossy. Stir in the vanilla off the heat.

  8. Sauce and serve. Poke the warm sponge all over with a skewer and pour over half the warm sauce. Rest 10 minutes. Serve warm with the remaining sauce.

Curly Chef notes

  • Why it can’t fail: dates and yogurt bind and moisten the crumb, and the toffee sauce forgives any dry edge.
  • Don’t overbake — moist crumbs on the skewer is the target, not a clean skewer.
  • Make ahead: the sauce keeps 5 days refrigerated; rewarm gently before serving.
  • Serve with vanilla ice cream or a pour of double cream.

Curly Chef standard: eggless · foolproof · restaurant-style comfort

Read the recipe
New recipe · Foolproof

Eggless Saffron Milk Cake

Golden, fragrant and impossibly moist — a celebration cake that soaks up its own sauce.

Makes9 squares
Bake175°C / 155°C fan, 30–35 min
Tin20 cm square, lined

Ingredients

Saffron threads0.5 g (a generous pinch)
Warm milk, for steeping30 g
Whole milk240 g
Unsalted butter60 g
Sweetened condensed milk200 g
Plain full-fat yogurt100 g
Plain flour220 g
Baking powder10 g (2½ tsp)
Fine sea salt3 g
Ground cardamom2 g

Saffron soak

Whole milk300 g
Sweetened condensed milk100 g
Saffron threads0.25 g

Method

  1. Steep the saffron. Soak 0.5 g saffron in 30 g warm milk for 15 minutes until deeply golden.

  2. Heat the oven to 175°C / 155°C fan. Line the tin.

  3. Hot milk base. Heat the 240 g milk and butter in a saucepan until steaming and the butter has melted — do not boil hard. Stir in the saffron milk.

  4. Whisk the binders. Whisk the condensed milk and yogurt in a large bowl until smooth, then pour in the hot saffron milk and whisk to combine.

  5. Fold the dries. Sift the flour, baking powder, salt and cardamom over the bowl and whisk gently until just smooth — a few small lumps are fine.

  6. Bake. Pour into the tin and bake 30–35 minutes until deep golden and a skewer comes out clean.

  7. Warm the soak. Heat the 300 g milk, 100 g condensed milk and 0.25 g saffron until steaming.

  8. Soak and chill. While the cake is warm, poke it all over with a skewer and pour the soak slowly over the top. Rest 30 minutes, then chill 2 hours. Serve chilled, scattered with chopped pistachios.

Curly Chef notes

  • Why it can’t fail: the hot-milk method gives an even, tight crumb, and the soak rescues any hint of dryness.
  • Don’t skip the poking — the soak must reach the centre of the cake.
  • Make ahead: keeps 3 days refrigerated; the flavour deepens overnight.
  • Finish with 20 g finely chopped pistachios and dried rose petals if you like.

Curly Chef standard: eggless · foolproof · bakery classic, elevated

Dark Chocolate Tiffin

Crushed biscuits, fruit and nuts under dark chocolate — the 20-minute slice that never fails.

Read the recipe
New recipe · Foolproof · No-bake

Dark Chocolate Tiffin

No oven, no setting agents, no stress — the fridge does all the work.

Makes16 squares
MethodNo-bake — 20 min hands-on
ChillAt least 4 hours
Tin20 cm square, lined

Ingredients

Dark chocolate, 55–60%300 g, chopped
Unsalted butter100 g
Golden syrup60 g
Digestive biscuits250 g, broken into rough 2 cm pieces
Raisins80 g
Toasted hazelnuts60 g, roughly chopped (optional)
Fine sea salt2 g
Cocoa powderfor dusting

Method

  1. Line the tin with cling film or parchment, leaving overhanging edges to lift the tiffin out.

  2. Melt. Melt the chocolate, butter and golden syrup in a heatproof bowl over barely simmering water (or in the microwave in 30-second bursts), stirring until completely glossy.

  3. Mix. Stir in the salt, then the biscuits, raisins and hazelnuts — every piece should be coated in chocolate.

  4. Set. Tip into the tin, press down firmly and level the top. Chill at least 4 hours until completely solid.

  5. Serve. Lift out, dust with cocoa and cut into 16 squares with a hot, dry knife.

Curly Chef notes

  • Why it can’t fail: there is no baking and no setting agent — if you can melt chocolate, you can make this.
  • Keep the biscuit pieces chunky — crumbs turn to mush; 2 cm pieces give the classic crunch.
  • Make ahead: keeps 2 weeks in an airtight box in the fridge.
  • Swap freely: dried cranberries, glacé cherries or mixed peel all work in place of raisins.

Curly Chef standard: eggless · foolproof · no-bake
